newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO tries to stop bombing spree in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO tries to stop bombing spree in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO commanders held talks with Bosnian leaders on Monday to try to halt a spate of bombing and arson attacks apparently aimed at preventing refugees from returning to their homes.

U.S. Admiral Joseph Lopez, commander of the NATO peace force in Bosnia, met Moslem and Croat members of the country's new collective presidency on Monday urging their help in ending the communal violence, a NATO spokesman said.
Lopez held a similar meeting with the Serb member of Bosnia's presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, on Saturday.
NATO condemned the destruction of scores of homes in northwest Bosnia last week, saying the incidents appeared to be well-orchestrated attacks.
More than 90 Moslem houses and two mosques were destroyed in several abandoned villages near Serb-held Prijedor in the course of several hours last week.
In Croat-held Drvar to the south, 65 Serb houses in two villages were torched over several days.
Major Brett Boudreau said the demolition around Prijedor appeared systematic. Several 10 kg (20 pound) anti-tank mines were rigged to each house, he said.
"It is nothing but self-destructive to mine the rubble, to torch the ruins, to further damage properties that some needy refugees of any ethnicity might be able to fix up and move into," he said.
Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative in Bosnia, inspected settlements in the northwest region on Sunday and found houses still smoking.
NATO said a Serb village was burned in Croat-held territory near the western town of Drvar, the second settlement to be torched in recent weeks.
Under a U.S.-brokered peace accord signed last December, Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders agreed to guarantee refugees the right to return to their homes.
But during 10 months of peace only a small number of people dared to cross back to territory controlled by another ethnic group.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees has been struggling to rebuild trust between divided communities.
The UNHCR sponsors bus lines that bring people across former front lines but it is constantly hampered by nationalists unwilling to renounce their ethnically pure territories.

A UNHCR-sponsored bus route between Prijedor and the Moslem-held town of Sanski Most sparked tit-for-tat incidents earlier last week when Moslems beat up a group of Serbs and arrested a Serb man who was visiting his former village.
Destruction of already damaged and abandoned property followed, setting back plans to bring Moslems back to at least one village around Prijedor.
NATO has stepped up patrols to try to combat the destruction of houses in sensitive areas and catch bombers.
